title: The Berlin Airlift
text:
In June 1948 the Soviet Union cut all road, rail and canal routes into the western sectors of Berlin, leaving about two million people with weeks of food and coal. The Western allies decided to supply the city entirely by air, something many experts thought impossible.

At first the airlift was improvised. At the end of July the American general William Tunner, who had run the wartime airlift over the Himalayas, took command. On 13 August, a day of bad weather later called Black Friday, planes stacked up over Tempelhof airport, circling in the clouds while crews on the ground tangled with crashed and blocked aircraft. Tunner, caught in the stack himself, turned the operation into an assembly line. Planes flew in strict corridors at fixed altitudes and intervals. A pilot who missed his landing did not try again; he flew straight back to base with his load so that the stream behind him was never disrupted. Ground crews and German workers unloaded aircraft in minutes.

The pace kept rising. Berliners themselves, many of them women, built a new airfield at Tegel in about three months. On 16 April 1949 the airlift made an Easter parade of nearly 1,400 flights in twenty-four hours, almost one a minute.

The Soviets lifted the blockade in May 1949. By the time the airlift ended that autumn, the American, British and allied crews had flown in more than two million tons of supplies. Dozens of airmen died in crashes.
lesson: Huge efforts succeed through relentless coordination: clear rules, steady rhythm and everyone knowing exactly where they fit. Discipline in the system beats heroics.
people: Lucius Clay, William Tunner, allied aircrews, Berliners
source: William H. Tunner, Over the Hump (1964); US Air Force historical studies of the Berlin Airlift
